o: Sum over all non-empty subsets S of nums of max(S)² · min(S), modulo 1e9+7. Brute force is exponential; n up to 1e5 demands a combinatorial formula. Sorting helps: after sorting ascending, fix the maximum as the element at index i; every subset containing i with all other indices ≤ i has max = nums[i], and its min is whichever smallest index was included.
k: Sort ascending; fixing the largest index i determines the max of the group.
Among subsets containing i using indices ≤ i, the number with minimum exactly nums[j] (j ≤ i) is 2^(i−j−1) (include j and i, exclude everything strictly between).
A running sum prev = Σ_{j<i} nums[j]·2^(i−1−j) lets each contribution be computed in O(1), updated as prev ← nums[i] + 2·prev.

a.i: Sort ascending. For each i, the total min-sum over groups whose max is nums[i] is nums[i] + prev, where prev accumulates Σ nums[j]·2^(i−1−j). Contribution: nums[i]² · (nums[i] + prev), all mod 1e9+7; then update prev.
s: For each x in sorted order: cur = (x + 2·prev) mod p; ans += x² · cur mod p; prev = cur.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the summation pass is linear.

w: Verification on [2,1,4]: sorted [1,2,4] gives contributions 1, 4·3=12, 16·8=128 → 141 ✓. The exponent bookkeeping (why it's 2^(i−j−1), not 2^(i−j)) is the classic pitfall — test on a 3-element array by hand. Duplicates are handled naturally by the index-based argument. A follow-up: replace max²·min with max·min·sum, needing a second running aggregate.
